item.title: Ideal activation func
item.description:
An ideal activation function must balance mathematical expressivity, numerical stability, optimization dynamics, and hardware efficiency. In practice, no single function optimizes all criteria simultaneously, which is why modern architectures favor specific trade-offs (e.g., SwiGLU in LLMs, ReLU in low-power CNNs).

The core characteristics that govern effective activation functions are:

1. Non-Linearity

  • Why it matters: The primary purpose of an activation function is to break linearity. Stacking purely linear layers W2(W1x+b1)+b2W_2(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2W2​(W1​x+b1​)+b2​ collapses to a single affine transform W′x+b′W' x + b'W′x+b′.
  • The ideal condition: Non-linear behavior across the dynamic operating range ensures the network satisfies the Universal Approximation Theorem, allowing it to model arbitrary complex continuous functions.

2. Resistance to Vanishing and Exploding Gradients

  • Non-Saturating on Positive Regime: The derivative should not decay to zero as activations grow large (x≫0x \gg 0x≫0).
    • Sigmoid and tanh⁡\tanhtanh fail here because lim⁡x→∞f′(x)=0\lim_{x \to \infty} f'(x) = 0limx→∞​f′(x)=0, causing backpropagated gradients ∏l=1L∂a(l)∂z(l)\prod_{l=1}^L \frac{\partial a^{(l)}}{\partial z^{(l)}}∏l=1L​∂z(l)∂a(l)​ to vanish exponentially through deep layers.
      • Functions like ReLU, GELU, and SiLU remain unbounded above (f(x)→∞f(x) \to \inftyf(x)→∞ as x→∞x \to \inftyx→∞), preserving unit or near-unit gradient magnitude.
  • Bounded Below: While the positive side should be unbounded, being bounded below (e.g., asymptoting near 0 or a small negative constant) acts as implicit L2L_2L2​ regularization, preventing positive feedback loops and activations blowing up to +∞+\infty+∞.

3. Smoothness and Differentiability (C1C^1C1 Continuity)

  • Smooth Loss Surfaces: Functions with a continuous, smooth first derivative (C1C^1C1 smooth, like GELU, SiLU, and Softplus) generate smoother loss landscapes compared to piecewise linear functions with sharp corners (like ReLU at x=0x = 0x=0).
  • Optimizer Compatibility: First-order momentum-based optimizers (AdamW, RMSprop) navigate smooth curvature more reliably without oscillating across sharp sub-gradient discontinuities.

4. Zero-Centered Outputs

  • Gradient Direction Alignment: Consider the gradient of the loss with respect to weight wiw_iwi​: ∂L∂wi=∂L∂z⋅xi \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} \cdot x_i ∂wi​∂L​=∂z∂L​⋅xi​ If an activation function produces strictly positive outputs (xi>0x_i > 0xi​>0, like standard Sigmoid or ReLU), all incoming weight gradients ∂L∂wi\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i}∂wi​∂L​ share the same sign as ∂L∂z\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}∂z∂L​.
  • The Consequence: Weights connected to that neuron can only update strictly in the all-positive or all-negative direction within a single batch, forcing a slow, inefficient zig-zagging trajectory during optimization.
  • Zero-centered functions (tanh⁡\tanhtanh, ELU, Leaky ReLU) allow balanced positive and negative gradient updates.

5. Non-Monotonicity (details)

  • The “Dip” Phenomenon: Historically, monotonicity (f′(x)≥0f'(x) \ge 0f′(x)≥0) was assumed to be an indispensable requirement for convex-like behavior. However, modern research (GELU, Swish/SiLU, Mish) demonstrated that slight non-monotonicity improves generalization.
  • Mechanism: In GELU and SiLU, the function dips slightly into negative territory (minimum around x≈−0.75x \approx -0.75x≈−0.75, y≈−0.17y \approx -0.17y≈−0.17 to −0.28-0.28−0.28) before climbing back to zero for large negative inputs. This small curvature preserves gradient flow for weakly negative values while suppressing extreme negative noise, avoiding the hard cutoff of ReLU.

6. Avoidance of “Dying Neurons”

  • If a function has a completely flat zero-gradient region (f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 for all x<0x < 0x<0, as in ReLU), a large bias or weight update can shift the neuron permanently into the inactive region.
  • Once stuck, the gradient is 0 across all future inputs, rendering the parameter permanently un-trainable.
  • An ideal function either retains a small non-zero slope for negative inputs (Leaky ReLU: αx\alpha xαx) or smoothly asymptotes with a decaying derivative (ELU, SiLU).

7. Computational and Hardware Efficiency

  • FLOPs vs. Memory Bandwidth: Activation functions are typically memory-bandwidth-bound elementwise operations in GPU kernels.
    • Evaluating complex transcendental functions (exp⁡(x)\exp(x)exp(x), erf(x)\text{erf}(x)erf(x), trigonometric functions) requires many more instruction cycles than simple comparisons (max⁡(0,x)\max(0, x)max(0,x)).
      • However, with modern hardware accelerator fused kernels (like Triton or CUDA operator fusion), the cost of evaluating SiLU or GELU approximations is largely amortized, making them the standard choice for LLMs despite being more compute-heavy than ReLU.

8. Bilinear and Gating Capability (Modern Architectures)

  • In large language models and modern transformers, isolated scalar functions are increasingly replaced by Gated Linear Units (GLUs) like SwiGLU.
  • Multiplicative Routing: An ideal modern activation block supports bilinear interactions (f(xW1)⊙xW2)(f(xW_1) \odot xW_2)(f(xW1​)⊙xW2​), allowing features to selectively amplify or suppress each other dynamically with dual gradient backpropagation pathways: ∇x=∇f(u)⊙v+f(u)⊙∇v \nabla_x = \nabla f(u) \odot v + f(u) \odot \nabla v ∇x​=∇f(u)⊙v+f(u)⊙∇v This prevents gradient bottlenecks even if one branch becomes saturated.

item.title: Non monotonicity
item.description:
What Monotonicity Means

A function f(x)f(x)f(x) is monotonic if its output never moves in the opposite direction of its input. If x1≤x2x_1 \le x_2x1​≤x2​, then f(x1)≤f(x2)f(x_1) \le f(x_2)f(x1​)≤f(x2​) everywhere (non-decreasing). In terms of calculus, its first derivative is always non-negative:

f′(x)≥0for all x f'(x) \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } x f′(x)≥0for all x

Classic activation functions are monotonic:

  • ReLU: max⁡(0,x)\max(0, x)max(0,x) — flat at 000, then strictly increases with slope 111.
  • Sigmoid: σ(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}σ(x)=1+e−x1​ — strictly increases from 000 toward 111.
  • Tanh: strictly increases from −1-1−1 toward 111.

A non-monotonic activation function violates this rule: its derivative changes sign. As xxx increases, f(x)f(x)f(x) may decrease, hit a local minimum, and then increase.

The Non-Monotonic Behavior in Practice

Modern activation functions like SiLU / Swish and GELU are non-monotonic:

  • SiLU: f(x)=x⋅σ(x)=x1+e−xf(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x) = \frac{x}{1 + e^{-x}}f(x)=x⋅σ(x)=1+e−xx​
  • GELU: f(x)=x⋅Φ(x)≈x⋅σ(1.702x)f(x) = x \cdot \Phi(x) \approx x \cdot \sigma(1.702 x)f(x)=x⋅Φ(x)≈x⋅σ(1.702x)

Where the Dip Occurs

Take the derivative of SiLU(x)=x⋅σ(x)\text{SiLU}(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x)SiLU(x)=x⋅σ(x):

f′(x)=σ(x)+x⋅σ′(x)=σ(x)+x⋅σ(x)(1−σ(x))=σ(x)(1+x(1−σ(x))) f'(x) = \sigma(x) + x \cdot \sigma'(x) = \sigma(x) + x \cdot \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x)) = \sigma(x)\Big(1 + x(1 - \sigma(x))\Big) f′(x)=σ(x)+x⋅σ′(x)=σ(x)+x⋅σ(x)(1−σ(x))=σ(x)(1+x(1−σ(x)))
  • For large positive xxx (x→+∞x \to +\inftyx→+∞): σ(x)→1\sigma(x) \to 1σ(x)→1, so f′(x)→1f'(x) \to 1f′(x)→1. It acts like ReLU (f(x)≈xf(x) \approx xf(x)≈x).
  • For large negative xxx (x→−∞x \to -\inftyx→−∞): σ(x)→0\sigma(x) \to 0σ(x)→0, so f(x)→0f(x) \to 0f(x)→0 and f′(x)→0f'(x) \to 0f′(x)→0. Extreme negative inputs are suppressed.
  • Near zero on the negative side (x∈[−2,0]x \in [-2, 0]x∈[−2,0]):
    • At x=0x = 0x=0: f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0 and f′(0)=0.5>0f'(0) = 0.5 > 0f′(0)=0.5>0.
      • At x=−1x = -1x=−1: σ(−1)≈0.2689\sigma(-1) \approx 0.2689σ(−1)≈0.2689. f′(−1)=0.2689⋅[1+(−1)(1−0.2689)]=0.2689⋅[1−0.7311]=0.2689⋅0.2689≈0.072>0f'(-1) = 0.2689 \cdot [1 + (-1)(1 - 0.2689)] = 0.2689 \cdot [1 - 0.7311] = 0.2689 \cdot 0.2689 \approx 0.072 > 0f′(−1)=0.2689⋅[1+(−1)(1−0.2689)]=0.2689⋅[1−0.7311]=0.2689⋅0.2689≈0.072>0.
      • Moving further left to x≈−1.28x \approx -1.28x≈−1.28: f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0. This is the local minimum, where f(−1.28)≈−0.278f(-1.28) \approx -0.278f(−1.28)≈−0.278.
      • For x∈(−∞,−1.28)x \in (-\infty, -1.28)x∈(−∞,−1.28): f′(x)<0f'(x) < 0f′(x)<0. As xxx becomes more negative, f(x)f(x)f(x) actually increases back toward 000 from below.

Because the derivative transitions from negative (x<−1.28x < -1.28x<−1.28) to zero (x≈−1.28x \approx -1.28x≈−1.28) to positive (x>−1.28x > -1.28x>−1.28), the function is non-monotonic.

Why Non-Monotonicity Helps Optimization

For decades, non-monotonicity was avoided because monotonic functions make single-layer optimization problems convex. However, deep networks are fundamentally non-convex, and the non-monotonic “bump/dip” offers three distinct mechanistic advantages:

1. Soft Thresholding Instead of a Hard Wall

ReLU applies a hard cutoff at zero:

  • If x=−0.001x = -0.001x=−0.001, output is 000, gradient is 000.
  • If x=+0.001x = +0.001x=+0.001, output is 0.0010.0010.001, gradient is 111.

This sharp cliff discards information immediately for any input slightly below zero.

A non-monotonic function like SiLU or GELU treats small negative values differently:

  • Mild negative values (x∈[−1,0]x \in [-1, 0]x∈[−1,0]) produce a small negative output (f(x)∈[−0.28,0]f(x) \in [-0.28, 0]f(x)∈[−0.28,0]) with a non-zero positive gradient.
  • The network can “change its mind”: if an incoming signal is slightly negative during early training, it is not immediately silenced. Gradients can still push the weight back into the active positive regime.
  • Large negative noise (x<−3x < -3x<−3) is pushed toward zero, maintaining noise suppression.

2. Negative Gradient Channel

Because f′(x)<0f'(x) < 0f′(x)<0 when x<−1.28x < -1.28x<−1.28, backpropagated error gradients flip sign:

∂L∂x=∂L∂f⋅f′(x) \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial f} \cdot f'(x) ∂x∂L​=∂f∂L​⋅f′(x)

When f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) is negative, an increase in upstream loss pulls the pre-activation xxx in the opposite direction compared to the positive regime. This introduces a self-stabilizing restorative force that prevents activations from drifting arbitrarily far into the negative regime.

3. Smoother Loss Landscapes

The non-monotonic dip naturally eliminates the sharp zero-crossing discontinuity (C0C^0C0 discontinuity in derivative) present in ReLU:

Empirical analysis by Li et al. (2018) on loss landscape visualization showed that replacing ReLU with smooth non-monotonic activations (like GELU or Swish) removes rugged, chaotic terrain full of bad local minima, replacing them with convex-like basins that gradient descent algorithms (AdamW) traverse significantly faster.
